newsitem.title: INDONESIA: FEATURE-Indonesia billionaire wants to give it away.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Indonesia billionaire wants to give it away.

text.p: Even for a nation where success in business is heavily dependent on who you know, Muhammad "Bob" Hasan's contacts in Indonesia are unbeatable.

Once a driver in central Java, Hasan, a short man with huge bags under his eyes, is now one of the country's wealthiest businessmen, President Suharto's golfing buddy and apparently his closest friend.
"We have known each other...for about 40 years," Hasan, 67, told Reuters this week during an interview in a remote part of East Kalimantan province on Indonesia's half of Borneo island.
Mangkajang is the site of a $1.3 billion pulp mill built by Hasan which Suharto inaugurated on Wednesday. Later, the two went off together on a deep-sea fishing trip.
"We see each other at least three or four times a week, playing golf...also (talking) about various things...because I am not a minister, I am a private entrepreneur," Hasan said.
"Definitely we have a close relationship."

When the two got to know each other, Hasan was a minor ethnic Chinese businessman and Suharto a powerful young officer in the army. According to Jakarta gossip, they struck up a relationship; Hasan's influence began to grow and he won some important logging concessions.
When Suharto became president of the Moslem-majority nation in the mid-1960s, Hasan was at his side.

Three decades and a conversion to Islam later, he virtually rules Indonesia's timber trade and admits he has stakes in about 300 domestic companies spread out through the country's sprawling economy, including banks, insurance, advertising, paper, copper, oil and media.
Forbes magazine's latest list of the world's wealthiest people had Hasan in 99th place with an estimated net worth of $3 billion. Suharto was placed sixth with $16 billion.
But now, Hasan says. he wants to give his money away. WANTS TO BE LIKE FORD OR ROCKEFELLER
Asked how rich he was, Hasan said: "I don't know. I can only eat three times a day.

"We are giving it back, we are giving it back to the foundations. We want our foundations to be like the Ford or Rockefeller foundations. So that when we are not around any more, the foundations can still help those who need help."

The two primary charity foundations, headed by Suharto but run by Hasan, are called Yayasan Supersumar, which provides free education to deserving children, and Yayasan Darmais, which runs homes and hospitals for the elderly, the disabled and the orphaned.
"It's my personal ambition to distribute my wealth," Hasan said. "Because there are still people living under the line of poverty."
Hasan is married and has adopted three children.
Friends say because Hasan was himself adopted in his childhood by General Gatot Subroto, one of Indonesia's best-known officers, he is particularly keen on charities which help poor children.

Sceptics however note that Nusamba, a company majority owned by the two charity foundations with Hasan and Suharto's eldest son controlling minor stakes, has been involved in two of Indonesia's biggest corporate shake-ups of the past year.

Both the takeover of the country's biggest automobile manufacturer, Astra International, and the Busang gold scandal cemented Hasan's role as a major powerbroker and virtually the corporate extension of Suharto, they say. FROM TIMBER TO CARS
Astra is a widely-held conglomerate with holdings scattered through Indonesia's powerful and wealthy.

Last year, tobacco tycoon Putera Sampoerna began accumulating Astra shares and quickly ran up the largest stake in the company. An uproar ensued, and the presidential palace signalled it was not pleased with the turn of events.
Within weeks, Sampoerna handed over much of his holdings in Astra to Nusamba at a slight profit and in February Hasan was named the company's president director.

"We thought we would just buy the shares because it was a good investment," Hasan said. He said it made business sense for the charities to invest in good companies, where returns were ensured, rather than lock up funds in interest-bearing accounts. THE DECEPTIVE POT OF GOLD
Until it was exposed as the biggest mining fraud of all time, the Busang gold field in East Kalimantan was the business most powerful Indonesians wanted to get into.

Owned by Canadian mining firm Bre-X Minerals Ltd, it was said to hold some 200 million ounces of gold, making it the richest find of the century. Suharto's two eldest children, daughter Siti Hardianti Rukmana and son Sigit Harjojudanto, joined opposite sides bidding to take over part of Bre-X's stake.

Hasan stepped in, brokering a deal for Nusamba and keeping the peace between the feuding siblings. It received a 30 percent stake in the property, Bre-X retained 45 percent and the Indonesian government 10 percent.
Freeport McMoRan Copper and Gold Inc, whose owner Jim Bob Moffett is a close associate of Hasan, was given the remainder.
Hasan told Reuters it was another business investment on behalf of the charities, but it went awry after a Freeport assay test found there was insignificant gold in the property.
"I thought all the big guys are there, it's safe. Anyway, we didn't spend anything. In business you either make money or you lose money. It doesn't change your life."
But golf, apparently, is a different ball game.
Asked who wins when he plays Suharto, Hasan's usually lugubrious face breaks into a smile which stretches under his drooping moustache.
"I have the lower handicap, I usually win," he said.
